subject: mathematics
title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027 (version 3, published May 2024)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings, their numbering and the Core/Extended split are transcribed from the official syllabus document. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; their numbering (subtopic code + .n) is ours and only loosely follows the order of the board's numbered statements. 'Extended:' marks objectives that only Extended candidates are examined on.
notes: Checked on 2026-10-07 against the official PDF (version 3, May 2024; 'Subject content', 'Assessment overview' and 'Changes to this syllabus'): all nine topics and 72 subtopic headings, the numbering, the Extended-only subtopics and the paper facts match.

Extended-only subtopics (Core shows 'Extended content only'): 1.17, 1.18, 2.3, 2.8, 2.12, 2.13, 3.4, 3.7, 4.8, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5, 6.6, 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 8.4, 9.6 and 9.7. These nodes are linked to Papers 2 and 4.

Heading differences between tiers: 4.7 is 'Circle theorems' (Core) and 'Circle theorems I' (Extended); 9.3 is 'Averages and range' (Core) and 'Averages and measures of spread' (Extended). The nodes use one heading and the description records the other.

Within shared subtopics the Core and Extended depth differs (e.g. 1.2 Venn diagrams with two or three sets, 2.6 inequalities, 2.7 sequences, 7.1 transformations, 8.3 combined events). A node cannot restrict a concept by tier, so Extended-only depth is recorded in the objectives ('Extended:') and content for it should say so.

Not in this syllabus (removed in 2025 or never included): linear programming, proper-subset notation, congruence criteria (only the term 'congruent' remains), constructions of perpendicular and angle bisectors, loci, logarithms, box-and-whisker plots, matrices, number bases. Concepts for these exist in the family registry for ZIMSEC and are deliberately not covered here.
2.2 item 5 (completing the square for an expression) is taught with the quadratic-equation concepts, which are covered on 2.5 Equations so that the quadratic topic test draws from one subtopic.
Paper facts (durations, marks, weightings, calculator rules) are from the 'Assessment overview' of the official document.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics develops fluency with number, algebra, graphs, coordinate geometry, geometry, mensuration, trigonometry, transformations and vectors, probability and statistics, and the ability to use them to solve problems in abstract and real-life contexts, with and without a calculator. Candidates follow either the Core curriculum or the Extended curriculum, which contains all of the Core content and more.
assessmentOverview: Core candidates take Paper 1 (non-calculator) and Paper 3 (calculator), each 1 hour 30 minutes and 80 marks; they can be awarded grades C to G. Extended candidates take Paper 2 (non-calculator) and Paper 4 (calculator), each 2 hours and 100 marks; they can be awarded grades A* to E. Each paper is worth half of the qualification, contains structured and unstructured questions, and includes a list of formulas.

routes.name: Core
routes.description: Papers 1 and 3. The highest grade available is C.

routes.name: Extended
routes.description: Papers 2 and 4. Grades A* to E are available.

objectives.text: Recognise and use natural numbers, integers, prime numbers, square and cube numbers, rational and irrational numbers and reciprocals.
Find common factors and common multiples, write a number as a product of its prime factors, and find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of numbers.
Write numbers given in words in figures, and numbers given in figures in words.

children.name: Sets
children.description: Core: Venn diagrams with at most two sets. Extended: at most three sets.

objectives.text: Describe sets with set language and notation, including listing, set-builder notation, the universal set, complement, union, intersection and number of elements.
Draw and interpret Venn diagrams with two sets to show the relationships between sets.
Extended: use element, subset and empty-set notation and Venn diagrams with up to three sets.
Calculate squares, square roots, cubes, cube roots and other powers and roots of numbers.
Recall the squares of the whole numbers 1 to 15 and the cubes of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10, together with the corresponding roots.
Use proper and improper fractions, mixed numbers, decimals and percentages in context, writing fractions in their simplest form.
Recognise equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages and convert between them.
Extended: use recurring-decimal notation and convert between recurring decimals and fractions.
Put numbers and quantities in order of size and use the symbols =, ≠, >, <, ≥ and ≤.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide integers, fractions, mixed numbers and decimals, including negative numbers.
Apply the correct order of operations, including brackets, and use negative numbers in practical situations such as temperature changes.
Evaluate numbers with positive, zero and negative integer indices.
Use the rules of indices to simplify and evaluate numerical expressions.
Extended: evaluate numbers with fractional indices.
Write numbers in the form A × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer, and convert them back to ordinary numbers.
Calculate with numbers in standard form (Core candidates do this on the calculator paper only).
Round values to a given number of decimal places or significant figures, or to the nearest whole number, ten, hundred or thousand.
Estimate the results of calculations with numbers, quantities and measurements, for example by rounding each number to one significant figure.
Give answers to a degree of accuracy that suits the context of a problem.
State the upper and lower bounds of a value that has been rounded to a given accuracy.
Extended: find the upper and lower bounds of the result of a calculation that uses rounded values.
Write ratios in their simplest form.
Share a quantity in a given ratio.
Use proportional reasoning and ratios in context, for example adapting recipes, using map scales and deciding which option is better value.
Calculate with common rates such as hourly rates of pay, exchange rates, flow rates and fuel consumption.
Use other rates such as density, pressure and population density when the formula is given.
Solve problems involving average speed, distance and time, using compound units such as m/s and km/h.
Find a percentage of a quantity and write one quantity as a percentage of another.
Calculate percentage increases and decreases in contexts such as profit and loss, discounts, deposits and earnings, including percentages over 100%.
Calculate simple interest and compound interest without being given a formula.
Extended: use reverse percentages to find an original amount, and work with repeated percentage changes.
Use a calculator efficiently, rounding only the final answer.
Enter values such as times correctly and interpret the calculator display in context, for example as an amount of money or a time.
Calculate with seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years, converting between units.
Convert between times on the 12-hour and 24-hour clocks.
Read clocks and timetables and solve problems involving time zones, local times and time differences.
Carry out calculations with money.
Convert an amount from one currency to another.
Extended: use exponential growth and decay, such as depreciation and population change, by applying a repeated multiplier.
Extended: simplify surds and expressions that contain surds.
Extended: rationalise the denominator of a fraction.
Understand that letters can stand for general numbers.
Substitute numbers into expressions and formulas and evaluate them.
Simplify expressions by collecting like terms.
Expand products of algebraic expressions, including two brackets (Extended: more than two brackets).
Factorise expressions fully by taking out common factors.
Extended: factorise by grouping, as a difference of two squares, as a perfect square, and expressions of the forms ax² + bx + c and ax³ + bx² + cx.
Extended: write an expression ax² + bx + c in completed-square form (taught with the quadratic equations of 2.5).
Extended: add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic fractions.
Extended: factorise and simplify rational expressions.
Use positive, zero and negative indices in algebraic expressions (Extended: also fractional indices).
Use the rules of indices to simplify algebraic expressions and to solve simple equations with the unknown in the index.
Form expressions, equations and formulas from information given in words or diagrams.
Solve linear equations in one unknown, including equations with brackets and fractions.
Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations in two unknowns.
Extended: solve simultaneous equations in which one equation is linear and the other is not.
Extended: solve quadratic equations by factorising.
Extended: solve quadratic equations by completing the square and by using the quadratic formula, giving answers to a stated degree of accuracy.
Change the subject of a formula (Core: the subject appears once and not as a power or root).
Extended: solve equations with fractions that have numerical or linear algebraic denominators.

children.name: Inequalities
children.description: Linear programming is not part of this syllabus.

objectives.text: Represent and interpret inequalities, including on a number line with open circles for strict and closed circles for inclusive inequalities.
Extended: form, solve and interpret linear inequalities, including double inequalities.
Extended: show linear inequalities in two variables as regions on a graph, with broken lines for strict and solid lines for inclusive inequalities, shading the unwanted region.
Extended: write down the inequalities that define a given region.
Continue a number sequence or pattern.
Recognise patterns in sequences, including term-to-term rules and relationships between different sequences.
Find and use the nth term of linear sequences and of simple quadratic and simple cubic sequences.
Extended: find and use the nth term of quadratic, cubic and exponential sequences and simple combinations of these, including subscript notation.
Extended: express direct and inverse proportion algebraically, including proportion to a square, cube, square root or cube root, using the ∝ symbol.
Extended: use an equation of proportion to find unknown quantities.
Use and interpret graphs in practical situations, including travel graphs and conversion graphs, and interpret the gradient of a straight-line graph as a rate of change.
Draw graphs from given data, such as a distance–time graph of a journey.
Extended: apply rate of change to distance–time and speed–time graphs, including acceleration and deceleration.
Extended: find the distance travelled as the area under a speed–time graph made of straight-line sections.
Complete tables of values and draw, recognise and interpret graphs of linear, quadratic and reciprocal functions with integer coefficients.
Solve equations graphically, including finding roots and using the intersection of a line and a curve.
Extended: draw and interpret graphs of functions made of up to three terms axⁿ (n = −2, −1, −½, 0, ½, 1, 2, 3) and of exponential functions, including graphs of exponential growth and decay.
Recognise, sketch and interpret graphs of linear and quadratic functions, showing roots and symmetry.

Extended: recognise, sketch and interpret cubic, reciprocal and exponential graphs, showing turning points, roots, symmetry and asymptotes, and find the turning point of a quadratic by completing the square.
Extended: estimate the gradient of a curve at a point by drawing a tangent.
Extended: differentiate functions of the form axⁿ, where n is a positive integer or zero, and sums of up to three such terms.
Extended: use differentiation to find gradients of curves and the coordinates of stationary (turning) points.
Extended: decide whether a turning point is a maximum or a minimum.
Extended: use function notation and understand the domain and range of a function.
Extended: find the inverse function f⁻¹(x).
Extended: form composite functions such as gf(x) = g(f(x)).
Plot and read Cartesian coordinates in two dimensions, in all four quadrants.
Draw the straight-line graph of a linear equation (Core: equations in the form y = mx + c unless a table of values is given).
Find the gradient of a straight line drawn on a grid.
Extended: calculate the gradient of a straight line from the coordinates of two points on it.
Extended: calculate the length of a line segment from the coordinates of its end points.
Extended: find the coordinates of the midpoint of a line segment.
Find and interpret the gradient and y-intercept of a straight line from its equation (Core: y = mx + c; Extended: also forms such as ax + by = c).
Find the equation of a straight line from its graph or from given information, in a fully simplified form.
Find the gradient and the equation of a straight line parallel to a given line.
Extended: find the gradient and the equation of a straight line perpendicular to a given line, including the perpendicular bisector of a line segment.

children.name: Geometrical terms
children.description: Candidates use the term 'congruent' but are not expected to show that two shapes are congruent.

objectives.text: Use and interpret geometrical terms such as vertex, parallel, perpendicular, bearing, acute, obtuse and reflex angles, interior and exterior angles, similar, congruent and scale factor (Extended: also plane and perpendicular bisector).
Use and interpret the vocabulary of triangles, special quadrilaterals, polygons, nets and solids.
Use and interpret the vocabulary of a circle, including radius, diameter, circumference, chord, tangent, arc, sector and segment.

children.name: Geometrical constructions
children.description: Constructions of perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors are not required, and loci are not part of this syllabus.

objectives.text: Measure and draw lines and angles accurately.
Construct a triangle from the lengths of its three sides using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, showing the construction arcs.
Draw, use and interpret nets of solids.
Draw and interpret scale drawings.
Use and interpret three-figure bearings measured clockwise from north.
Calculate lengths in similar shapes.
Extended: use the relationships between lengths and areas of similar shapes, and between lengths, surface areas and volumes of similar solids.
Extended: solve problems and give simple explanations involving similarity, including showing that two triangles are similar.
Recognise lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of two-dimensional shapes, including properties of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons linked to their symmetry.
Extended: recognise planes and axes of symmetry of prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones.
Calculate unknown angles using angles at a point, angles on a straight line, vertically opposite angles and the angle sums of triangles and quadrilaterals, giving reasons.
Calculate unknown angles formed with parallel lines using corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles, giving geometric reasons.
Use the interior and exterior angle properties of regular polygons (Extended: also irregular polygons).

children.name: Circle theorems I
children.description: Core heading: Circle theorems (angle in a semicircle and tangent–radius only).

objectives.text: Calculate unknown angles using the angle in a semicircle and the right angle between a tangent and a radius, giving reasons.
Extended: calculate unknown angles using the angle at the centre, angles in the same segment, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral and the alternate segment theorem, giving reasons.

Extended: use the symmetry properties of circles: equal chords are the same distance from the centre, the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre, and the two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
Use metric units of length, mass, area, volume and capacity in practical situations.
Convert quantities between larger and smaller metric units, including units of area and volume and between volume and capacity.
Calculate the perimeter and area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms and trapezia.
Calculate the circumference and area of a circle, including answers in terms of π.
Calculate arc lengths and sector areas as fractions of the circumference and area of a circle (Core: sector angles that are factors of 360°; Extended: any angle, including major sectors).
Calculate surface areas and volumes of cuboids, prisms and cylinders and solve problems involving them.
Calculate surface areas and volumes of spheres, pyramids and cones, using the formulas given, and solve problems involving them.

children.name: Compound shapes and parts of shapes

objectives.text: Calculate perimeters and areas of compound shapes and of parts of shapes.
Calculate surface areas and volumes of compound solids and of parts of solids (Extended: including frustums).
Know Pythagoras' theorem and use it to find a side of a right-angled triangle.
Use the sine, cosine and tangent ratios of acute angles to find sides and angles of right-angled triangles, giving angles to one decimal place.
Solve two-dimensional problems using Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry, including problems with bearings.
Extended: know that the perpendicular distance from a point to a line is the shortest distance to the line.
Extended: solve problems involving angles of elevation and depression.
Extended: recall the exact values of sin x and cos x for x = 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and of tan x for x = 0°, 30°, 45° and 60°.
Extended: recognise, sketch and interpret the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Extended: solve trigonometric equations in sin x, cos x or tan x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Extended: use the sine rule and the cosine rule to find lengths and angles in any triangle, including obtuse angles and the ambiguous case.
Extended: use the formula area = ½ab sin C.
Extended: solve problems in three dimensions using Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry, including the angle between a line and a plane.
Recognise, describe fully and draw reflections of shapes in a straight line (Core: vertical or horizontal lines).
Recognise, describe fully and draw rotations through multiples of 90° (Core: about the origin, a vertex or the midpoint of an edge of the shape).
Recognise, describe fully and draw enlargements from a centre by a scale factor (Core: positive and fractional scale factors; Extended: also negative scale factors).
Recognise, describe and draw translations by a column vector.
Extended: work with combinations of transformations.
Extended: describe a translation with a column vector, a directed line segment such as AB or a bold letter.
Extended: add and subtract vectors and multiply a vector by a scalar.
Extended: calculate the magnitude of a column vector as √(x² + y²).
Extended: represent vectors by directed line segments and use position vectors.
Extended: express vectors in terms of two coplanar vectors using sums and differences of vectors.
Extended: use vectors to reason and solve geometric problems, such as showing that lines are parallel or that three points are collinear.
Use the probability scale from 0 to 1.
Calculate the probability of a single event, giving it as a fraction, decimal or percentage.
Use the fact that the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability that it happens.
Extended: use probability notation such as P(A) and P(A′).
Use relative frequency as an estimate of probability, and understand the terms fair, biased and random.
Calculate expected frequencies.
Calculate probabilities of combined events using sample space diagrams, Venn diagrams and tree diagrams (Core: with replacement only, Venn diagrams with two sets).
Extended: calculate probabilities of combined events without replacement.
Extended: calculate conditional probabilities from Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and tables.
Classify and tabulate statistical data, for example in tally tables and two-way tables.
Read, interpret and draw inferences from tables and statistical diagrams.
Compare sets of data using tables, graphs, averages and measures of spread.
Recognise the limits on the conclusions that can be drawn from given data.

children.name: Averages and range
children.description: Extended heading: Averages and measures of spread.

objectives.text: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of individual data in a list or ungrouped frequency table, and choose the average that suits a purpose.
Extended: calculate the quartiles and interquartile range of individual data.
Extended: estimate the mean of grouped discrete or continuous data and identify the modal class.
Draw and interpret bar charts (including composite and dual bar charts), pie charts, pictograms, ordered stem-and-leaf diagrams with a key, and simple frequency distributions.
Draw and interpret scatter diagrams and describe positive, negative and zero correlation.
Draw a straight line of best fit by eye, interpret it and use it to estimate values.
Extended: draw and interpret cumulative frequency tables and diagrams.
Extended: estimate and interpret the median, percentiles, quartiles and interquartile range from a cumulative frequency diagram.
Extended: draw and interpret histograms, including histograms with unequal class widths.
Extended: calculate with frequency density (frequency ÷ class width).
